The oath comes out of you slow and loud, *on Dargan's blood, and the blood of my clan*, and every spear in the room settles into the stillness of men hearing a thing they expected to hear. On the word *clan* you plant your feet and heave.

The desk is oak and iron-bound, and it lifts like a door in a gale. The ring on your chain comes up with it, and you roar "HOME!" and throw it. It goes over in one long crash. The lamp, the pen and the open ledger go down together in a spill of burning oil. The Foreman has no time to cry out. The edge of the desk comes down across his chest and he goes under it with the beads still in his fist, and he does not move again.

The ledger lands splayed open at your feet. You see Gorrak Vael's page before the flames take the corner of it: a column of years, each payment struck through in a clerk's neat hand, and the sum at the bottom rubbed out and rewritten in fresher ink every time, so that it never once reached nothing. He was never in debt. He was kept.

Tessa is already moving. She kicks the book into the burning oil, hauls its pages apart with her boot and her bound hands, and the fire climbs through it with a paper roar. Along the walls the six Tally-sworn are caught flat. Their mouths are open, their spears are still upright, and they have not yet understood that the man they came to watch swear is the man who just killed their master.

It is your turn again, and they are still stunned. You are at 1 hit point, still chained by both wrists to the ring on a toppled desk and hobbled at the ankle. The ledger burns at your feet, Tessa crouches beside it, and Gorrak is bound and watching from his pallet with his eye wide. Six spears stand between you and the barred door.

His past, which the opening must respect: he comes from a clan of mountain herders. When he was young, hobgoblins of the Iron Tallies warband, led by a tin-masked captain named Gorrak Vael (who notches a rod for every raid), overran his village. His father Dargan held the narrow Goat's Throat pass, losing a hand and then his life, so the herd and the children could flee; Korvash swore to him, with his blood on his hands, to protect the weak. His younger sister Tessa was lost in the raid and her fate is UNKNOWN: he never saw her fall and has never stopped wondering, so she must not be confirmed alive or dead unless discovered in play. The survivors fled to Harrowmere, where his aunt Veshra raised him and still sends word by travelers. The clan built a cairn at the Goat's Throat, which he has never had the heart to revisit. entries.text: notebook: updated The Greyshaft Foreman

Cold air touches your face first, then the smell of lamp-smoke and beeswax, and a pain that begins at your ribs and spreads. You surface into the same long low room. It is a little after two in the morning, and you have 1 hit point.

You remember how it went. You got as far as *On Dargan's blood* and gripped the table leg, and the singed-beard guard was already there with his sword. You never felt the blow. Your body was too tired to hold on to the thought.

The room is nearly as you left it. The stove is low. The lamp stands at the Foreman's elbow, unspilled, and the ledger is closed under his hand. Your wrists are chained to the table leg again, and the cuffs have rubbed fresh wounds over the old ones. Tessa sits against the far wall with the grey-eyed guard's spear laid across her knees like a bar. Her hood is down and her eyes are open, fixed on you. Gorrak lies on his pallet, awake, with his burned face turned to the wall.

The Foreman has not slept. His beads click slowly. "You have my admiration, Emberhide," he says, mildly, "and not my patience. The table was clever. The Draconic was less so." He opens the ledger to a fresh page and sets the pen beside it. "The rider leaves for the Border Stones at first light, in a little under five hours. He leaves whether you swear or not, unless you swear. Your sister's cords were cut as a courtesy, and I am not obliged to keep them cut."

Six spears stand along the walls, and the singed-beard guard watches you with a grin. The contract lies where it did, with one line struck out and the ink still wet at its foot. You have no weapon and no breath of fire, and the rage is long gone. Whatever you do next, the whole room is awake to watch it.

"I'll swear," I say, and I plant my feet, take hold of the table leg that holds my chains, and begin loud and slow: "On Dargan's blood, and the blood of my clan..."

Six guards are around you and the table, and three swords are drawn over you. The ledger is blackened but legible, a few paces from your reach. entries.text: notebook: updated The Greyshaft Foreman

You drag your feet and read the walk as you're hauled along it, but the cloud is low and the torches gutter, and the wind steals what you might have seen. You count six cloaks and a door, and little else. You lose the rest in the dark.

At the ledger-house door you plant your heels and say it flat and loud: you will hear his terms, but you will see Tessa alive and whole before you say a word.

It carries. A pause follows, and then the Foreman's small voice comes through the wood. "Open it. He's quite right."

The door swings in on lamp-smoke and the smell of scorched paper. The long room has been tidied. The table stands where it should, and the black scorch is scrubbed pale on the flags. The guard Guard 3 stands against the far wall with a bandaged arm, and Guard 6 is at his shoulder. Nobody else is left of the six who stood here at midnight. A new iron-bound chest sits on the desk, its lid raised an inch.

The Foreman sits behind it with his side freshly dressed and the beads in his fingers. He looks older, grey around the mouth, but his hands are as steady as ever. Beside him, on a stool, sits Tessa. Her hands are in her lap and unbound, and a needle and thread lie on a cloth at her knee. A bruise darkens one side of her face. She lifts her head, finds you, and holds your eyes. Her thumb presses once against her knee: *alive. Wait.*

"There," the Foreman says gently. "Whole, as she promised. I keep my word more often than you have been told." He gestures to a chair set in the middle of the floor. "Sit, Emberhide. You have been very expensive tonight, and I would like to know what I am buying."

The grey cloaks put you in the chair and stand behind it. Your wrists stay in iron. The dawn bell is a little under three hours away, and the Foreman has all the patience in the world. You have 1 hit point, a sister three paces off, and the floor.

entries.text: notebook: updated The Greyshaft Foreman

You plant your heels at the ledger-house door and say it flat and loud enough to carry through the wood: you will hear the Foreman's terms, but you will see Tessa alive and whole with your own eyes before you say a word.

On the climb you took in what you could with your head hanging. Six grey cloaks, two with crossbows slung. The gate-top walk has one barred stair door behind you and a wash-house roof to the left, with a drain-stair cut into the wall beyond it, the way you came before. The ledger-house shutters are latched from inside. Nobody tied your hobbles tight, and the chain between your wrists is short. The sergeant hears you and grunts. Whatever the Foreman wanted from you, he wants it with the door closed.

The door opens. Inside, the stove is lit and the long room smells of beeswax and scorched paper. The Foreman sits at the desk with the ledger open before him, its cover blackened and the edges brown. A knot shows at the back of her skull. She looks up at you and keeps sewing, but her eyes tell you that she is whole enough to bite.

You ask whether a safe-conduct is worth anything on a road his scouts watch, and who guards the mule. You make him read each clause again, ask for the surety to be named in a second hand, ask which witnesses will sign. You are slow, plain and stubborn, a herder haggling over a goat, and he takes it as that. He answers with the weary patience of a man who has haggled with worse. Twice he glances at the sand-glass on the desk. Both times you hand him another question before he can close the page. entries.text: notebook: updated Tessa

You plant your heels at the ledger-house door, and you say it flat and loud enough to carry through the wood: you'll hear the Foreman's terms, but you see Tessa alive and whole first.

You are not as sharp as you'd like. On the walk up you saw six grey cloaks, a bar on the outer door and a great deal of dark, and you came away with nothing you could use. You didn't mark the windows.

The demand lands, though. The door opens on the lit room. It is the same long low chamber, shutters closed, stove ticking, the scorch on the floor and the oak table back in its place. The sergeant gives a short nod, and the Foreman's small gentle voice answers from inside. "Of course. I would not ask a man to bargain blind."

Tessa sits on a stool by the stove with a bandage round her head, a needle in her hands and a spear across the knees of the guard beside her. She is sewing the long cut under the Foreman's ribs, where he sits half-stripped in his chair. She does not look up when you come in. The needle never stops. But her left hand, resting on his sleeve, makes the clan's sign against the cloth, thumb folded in: *I'm well.* Then it goes back to the thread.

The ledger lies on the desk, scorched brown along two edges, with a clasp now locked across it and the chest beside it. The key chain hangs at his belt. Four grey cloaks remain in the room, and two more stand behind you.

"You have seen her," the Foreman says. "She is whole. She is also useful, which is the reason she is whole. Sit him down." They put you on the floor against the table leg and fasten your chains again. The Foreman lifts a hand, and the brass beads click. "Your captain has been telling my men things tonight. It is unwise. Yet it is not you I mean to punish, Emberhide. I mean to buy you. Swear, and I will let you into the ledger yourself, once a season, to read your own count and his. I will even show you the page."

The shutters rattle in the wind. The dawn bell is still hours off. You are at 1 hit point, chained, with your sister three paces away, the Foreman at ease, and a clever question on your tongue. What does Korvash do?

entries.text: notebook: updated The Greyshaft Foreman

The walk up taught you what it could. There are six grey cloaks around you, all spears and no crossbows.
